rule: No view shows a predicted speedup, time-to-fill or ratio as a product claim. Numbers on this page are research findings, labelled with how they were measured.

findings.title: Competing trials barely slow each other within a site
findings.headline: Within the same site, the congestion elasticity is about 0.09 (95% CI 0.00 to 0.30), against the 1.0 our original model assumed.

tables.title: Coefficient on log(1 + overlapping competitors at the site)
rows: Pooled across sites (confounded by site type)
notes: Post hoc, not pre-registered: the pre-registered two-way variance clips negative eigenvalues of the whole coefficient covariance matrix (18 of 41 for the primary), so its se depends partly on how the controls are coded (0.104 as coded, 0.105 to 0.115 under equivalent codings); the coefficient's own two-way variance before clipping does not depend on the coding: se 0.087, 95% CI [-0.262, +0.077], p 0.29.

notes: 4 subsets were tested, so each subset's within-site CI is also shown at the Bonferroni level (alpha 0.05/4, z = 2.50); at that level the CIs that exclude zero: none; that exclude the full-sample estimate -0.093: none.

Subset estimates (for example sites with many earlier lung trials) are reported separately and are never used as the default.

findings.title: Allocation gains from coordination don't survive a time split
findings.headline: Coordination gains don't survive a time split: choosing with older trials and scoring with newer ones, the joint optimum is 1.02x each trial's best response in US-Northeast. Site selection alone (each trial's best response vs its registered sites) is 1.46x on the same split, scored by the same model rather than by observed enrollment.

findings.title: Site-level enrollment data is the binding constraint
findings.headline: Optimizing site selection needs site-level enrollment data, which is private today. Public registry data identifies site performance only weakly.
